title: Possible Effects of Nuclear War on Developing Countries

source.heading: UTME 2019 STRUCTURED QUESTIONS
source.directions: Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow.

passage.text: The evidence given so far demonstrates that a nuclear exchange in the Northern Hemisphere would have an unavoidable global aftermath making the continued existence of mankind impossible anywhere.
It is also very improbable that a nuclear exchange would be confined exclusively to the vicinity of the industrialised states.
Current developments indicate that a nuclear disaster would be carried into the territories of the developing countries in Asia, Africa and Latin America.

These developments include the preparations being made by aggressive forces for the armed seizure of the Middle East oil fields, the nuclear missile deployment in the South of Western Europe, the establishment of military bases of the Rapid Deployment of Forces in North Africa and the Indian Ocean, and the tensions in the South Atlantic and the Caribbean.

questions.stem: A suitable title for the passage is

options.text: Preparation for Nuclear War on the Third World Countries
options.why: The passage discusses both the likely global aftermath and how nuclear disaster would spread to developing nations, not just preparation.

options.text: Possible Effects of Nuclear War on Third World Countries
options.why: Sentences 1–4 focus on how a nuclear exchange would have fatal consequences and spread to developing countries in Asia, Africa and Latin America.

options.text: Strategies for a Nuclear Exchange
options.why: The passage warns against the danger of nuclear war rather than outlining battle strategies.

options.text: The Merits and Demerits of Nuclear Exchange
options.why: The passage presents no merits at all; it warns of global extinction.

options.text: militant
options.why: Sentence 4 links 'aggressive forces' with armed seizure of oil fields and military bases, matching 'militant'.

options.text: dissident
options.why: Dissident means rebelling against a government or policy, not preparing armed seizure.

options.text: reactionary
options.why: Reactionary refers to opposing political reform, not military aggression.

options.text: revolutionary
options.why: Revolutionary means seeking radical political change, which is not the military sense used here.

questions.stem: The central point being stressed in the passage is that

options.text: nuclear war is inevitable in the Third World countries
options.why: The passage warns of a likely spread if nuclear war occurs, not that it is already inevitable.

options.text: nuclear war is imminent in the Third World countries
options.why: Sentence 3 says current developments indicate it would be carried there, not that it is about to break out immediately.

options.text: a country does not have to be industrialised before being concerned with nuclear matters
options.why: While implied as a lesson, the passage directly emphasises the military build-up threatening developing regions.

options.text: the aggressive forces of the world are ready to carry the nuclear battle into the developing nations.
options.why: Sentences 3 and 4 directly state that nuclear disaster would be carried into developing countries through active military deployments.

questions.stem: According to the author, current world developments point to

options.text: an exclusive destruction of the developing countries
options.why: Sentence 1 says survival would become impossible anywhere, not only in developing countries.

options.text: a likely spread of nuclear calamity to the Third World
options.why: Sentence 3 explicitly states that current developments indicate a nuclear disaster would be carried into developing countries.

options.text: nuclear exchange taking place in Africa, Asia and Latin America
options.why: Sentence 1 begins with a nuclear exchange in the Northern Hemisphere spreading outward.

options.text: a confrontation between the industrialised and the developing countries.
options.why: The passage describes military deployments extending a Northern nuclear conflict into developing territories.

questions.stem: From this passage, we learn that nuclear exchange in the Northern Hemisphere would be

options.text: inconceivable
options.why: The writer treats a nuclear exchange as a real danger, not impossible to imagine.

options.text: inevitable
options.why: Sentence 1 says its aftermath would be unavoidable if it happened, not that the exchange itself is inevitable.

options.text: fatal to mankind
options.why: Sentence 1 states it would have an unavoidable global aftermath making the continued existence of mankind impossible anywhere.

options.text: partially destructive.
options.why: Making human existence impossible anywhere means total destruction, not partial.
